background.definition: Impetigo is a common, highly contagious, superficial skin infection that mainly affects children.

list.listitem: Incidence is 20/1000/y.
Incidence rates peak at 2 to 8 years of age.
Impetigo is the third most common skin disease in children, after eczema and viral warts.
It is the most common bacterial skin infection in children and is the most common skin infection in children between the ages of 2 years and 5 years.

A report showed high prevalence of impetigo in children in Aboriginal communities in northern Australia (49%), and in Pacific countries, specifically the Solomon Islands (52%), Fiji (36%) and Vanuatu (16%).
It is caused by direct inoculation of group A streptococci or S. aureus organisms into superficial cutaneous abrasions.
In nonbullous impetigo, neutrophilic vesicopustules are present within the epidermis.
The upper dermis contains an intense neutrophil and lymphocyte infiltrate.
In bullous impetigo, the staphylococcal exfoliative toxin causes exfoliative blisters locally at the site of infection.
There is cleavage of the desmoglein 1 complex which causes a split in the stratum granulosum and stratum spinosum layers of the upper epidermis.
There are few inflammatory cells and no bacteria in the blister cavity.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Close contacts such as in day care
Presence of underlying skin disease such as atopic dermatitis, tinea, or scabies

Differential.Differential_Features: Fewer crusts and pustules, Koebner phenomenon, itching
Painful, positive Tzanck smear, may have mucosal lesions
Age over 60, generalized eruption, tense blisters, palms and soles affected, positive direct immunofluorescence of skin
Recent drug exposure, may be generalized, may have mucous membrane ulceration
Pruritic papules at the site of the bites, may be urticarial
Thin-walled vesicles, lesions at different stages of healing present at the same time

list.listitem: The diagnosis of nonbullous impetigo is made based on the clinical findings of easily ruptured vesicles with thick, honey-colored crusting, with or without surrounding erythema or regional lymphadenopathy; these vesicles are located on the extremities or face.

The diagnosis of bullous impetigo is also made on clinical findings, including rapidly enlarging, flaccid bullae with sharp margins and no erythema, collarette scale at the periphery of ruptured lesions, and typical locations such as the diaper area, axillae, and neck folds.

Gram stain and culture are not considered unless the diagnosis is uncertain, there is no improvement, or there is concern regarding MRSA, or to identify patients with nephritogenic strains of Streptococcus during outbreaks of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Serologic antibody studies, such as antistreptolysin O titers, anti-DNase B, and antihyaluronidase can be ordered if the possibility of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis exists.
See .
No relevant clinical decision rules are found.

Mupirocin 2% ointment three times daily for 5 days and topical fusidic acid (not available in the U.S.) three times daily for 7 days are as, if not more, effective than oral antibiotics and are the recommended first-line treatment for localized impetigo. A
Other topical options include topical retapamulin 1% A and ozenoxacin 1%, B both dosed twice daily for 5 days.
The evidence is uncertain regarding the effectiveness of topical disinfectants like hydrogen peroxide in the acute treatment of impetigo. B

Oral antibiotics, such as dicloxacillin and cephalexin, are options in treating extensive impetigo, A and may be especially helpful during outbreaks of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis to eradicate nephritogenic strains of Streptococcus pyogenes. C

When methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aurues (MRSA) is suspected, consider treating impetigo with doxycycline, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, or clindamycin (if local clindamycin resistance is <10-15%). B
RCTs show consistent benefit of mupirocin and fusidic acid over placebo (NNT = 5) and equal efficacy to each other in 4 RCTs with 440 patients.

The resistance rates to topical fusidic acid are rising in Europe; studies showed up to 35% resistance in impetigo wound isolates of 133 patients in the south of the Netherlands, and rising rates of fusidic acid resistant S. aureus in impetigo and secondarily infected atopic dermatitis in Sweden.
The resistance rates to erythromycin are rising, and pooling of 10 studies with 581 patients found better cure rates of mupirocin compared with oral erythromycin (RR 1.07; 95% CI, 1.01-1.13).

A small study showed neomycin/bacitracin to be less effective compared to fusidic acid. Using neomycin and bacitracin for impetigo is not recommended due to their lower efficacy. Furthermore, they are among the most common causes of contact dermatitis among the various topical antibiotics.

In the 2012 Cochrane review evaluating interventions for impetigo, topical mupirocin appears superior to oral erythromycin, based on 10 RCTs involving 581 patients. Overall cure rates showed similar efficacy for topical and systemic antibiotics.
There is no good evidence that topical disinfectants such as chlorhexidine or hydrogen peroxide improve impetigo.

Another topical antibiotic, retapamulin (1% ointment twice daily), was shown to be better than placebo in effecting a clinical response in patients with impetigo (85.6% vs 52.1%; P < .0001) in one multicenter RCT. Retapamulin belongs to the class of pleuromutilin antibiotics (a derivative of the naturally occurring pleuromutilin produced by an edible mushroom) that inhibit bacterial protein synthesis. It is applied twice daily for 5 days and indicated use is limited to impetigo covering ≤100 cm2 in total area in adults or ≤2% of total body surface area in children ≥9 months old.
A double-blinded RCT showed equal efficacy of 1% retapamulin ointment and oral cephalexin in the treatment of secondarily infected dermatitis.

A topical nonfluorinated quinolone, ozenoxacin 1% cream twice daily for 5 days was superior to placebo for impetigo (success rate 35% vs 19%; P = 0.003). Ozenoxacin produced more rapid microbiological clearance than retapamulin Another RCT showed superior clinical and microbiological success compared with placebo and was well tolerated. It is approved in the US for patients aged 2 months and older. Use should be limited to areas less than 100 cm2. No pricing is available as this drug is a limited distribution drug, available only at specialty pharmacies.

Among the different oral antibiotics, penicillin appears inferior to erythromycin based on two studies involving 79 patients (pooled RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.07-1.56). Similarly, penicillin appears inferior to cloxacillin based on two studies involving 166 patients (pooled RR 1.59, 95% CI 1.21-2.08).
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole achieved microbiological clearance and healing of sores in 7 of 7 children from which beta-hemolytic streptococci and community-associated MRSA were cultured.
Oral antibiotics had more side effects than topical antibiotics, particularly gastrointestinal, but event rates were low overall.
There were no studies of patients with widespread impetigo or systemic symptoms; it is unclear if oral antibiotics are superior to topical antibiotics for people with extensive impetigo.
A small nonrandomized comparative trial showed equal efficacy of 5% black tea extract (Thea assamica) compared with topical and oral antibiotics.

Another small randomized trial showed efficacy of 4% tea tree oil nasal ointment and 5% tea tree oil body wash compared with 2% mupirocin nasal ointment and triclosan body wash for eradication of MRSA. Only 18 of 30 patients completed the trial.
There is insufficient evidence to support the efficacy of Chinese herbal medicines to treat impetigo or other skin and soft tissue infections.
Nonbullous impetigo may resolve spontaneously without treatment in 2 to 3 weeks, but adequate treatment results to faster healing. C
A systematic review showed symptomatic resolution in nonbullous impetigo at 7 days in 13-74% of patients without antibiotic treatment, with about one quarter not improving. B
The evidence supporting the efficacy of treating impetigo to prevent poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is unclear. C
Uncertainty exists regarding the role of impetigo in the development of rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease. C
Local wound care includes removing crusts with warm compresses and applying emollients on dry skin.
Ensure proper hand washing after treatment.
Cut fingernails short.
Avoid sharing towels, equipment, and other fomites.

National Collegiate Athletic Association and National Federation of State High School Associations rules state that a wrestler must be free of new lesions for 48 hours before competition; have received at least 72 hours of antibiotic therapy; and demonstrate no moist, exudative or purulent lesions. Occluding active lesions is disallowed.

feature.caption: Diagnosis of Impetigo.
feature.feature_body:
Clinical Features
Nonbullous impetigo
Begins as macules or papules that become transient superficial small vesicles on an erythematous base Erosions; secondary crust formation from dried serum Golden-yellow crusts often seen but not pathognomonic Scattered discrete lesions, may become confluent Satellite lesions outside the periphery Commonly affects face around nose and mouth, scalp, also limbs May occur anywhere, except palms and soles in secondary impetiginization Pruritus or soreness may be present Regional lymphadenopathy common
Bullous impetigo
Larger vesicles and flaccid bullae, commonly 1-2 cm; no erythematous halo More common in intertriginous sites May occur anywhere, including palms, soles, and buccal mucous membrane May form circinate lesions with "collarette" scale after central healing and peripheral spread Often seen in newborns and infants
